topics.h: Your school bag, the electricity in your fan and the dal on your plate all began as something in nature — but nature alone does not make a resource!
p: A resource is anything in our environment that can satisfy our needs, provided it is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable.
Things become resources through human activity: people use technology and knowledge to turn nature's materials into useful goods and services.
By origin, resources are biotic (from the biosphere and having life, such as forests, fisheries and livestock) or abiotic (non-living, such as rocks and metals).

By exhaustibility, they are renewable (can be renewed or reproduced, such as solar energy, wind and forests) or non-renewable (form over very long geological times, such as coal, petroleum and minerals).
By ownership they are individual, community, national or international; by status of development they are potential, developed, stock or reserves.

ex.q: Strong winds blow across the deserts of Rajasthan, but only a part of this wind is being used to make electricity. How would you classify this wind as a resource?
st: Origin: wind is non-living, so it is abiotic.
Exhaustibility: wind keeps blowing and is not used up, so it is renewable.
Status of development: it exists in the region but is not yet fully used, so it is a potential resource.
ex.a: Abiotic, renewable and (for the unused part) a potential resource.

topics.rl: The park in your colony where everyone plays cricket is a community resource, while your family's own bicycle is an individual resource.

topics.h: If one family grabs all the water in a village well, the others go thirsty. Resources must be planned for everyone — including people not yet born!
p: Using resources carelessly has caused problems: depletion of resources to satisfy the greed of a few, resources piling up in a few hands (dividing society into haves and have-nots), and global crises such as global warming, ozone layer depletion, pollution and land degradation.
Sustainable development means development without damaging the environment and without compromising the needs of future generations. The Brundtland Commission Report (1987) introduced this idea.

At the Rio de Janeiro Earth Summit in Brazil (June 1992), more than 100 heads of state met and adopted Agenda 21, a plan for global sustainable development; every local government should draw its own local Agenda 21.

Resource planning in India has three steps: (1) identifying and making an inventory of resources by surveying, mapping and estimating them; (2) building a planning structure with the right technology, skills and institutions; (3) matching resource development plans with overall national development plans.
Having resources is not enough: development also needs matching technology and institutions. Mahatma Gandhi said, 'There is enough for everybody's need and not for anybody's greed.'

ex.q: Arunachal Pradesh has plenty of water but is less developed than some regions with less water. What does this tell us about resources and development?
st: Arunachal Pradesh has abundant water resources.
But it lacks infrastructure (roads, power lines, industries) to use them fully.
So availability of a resource alone does not bring development; technology, infrastructure and institutions are also needed.
ex.a: Resources lead to development only when they are matched with suitable technology, infrastructure and planning.

topics.rl: When your housing society plants trees, saves water and shares one bus for school instead of ten cars, it is practising sustainable development.

topics.h: Your food, your home and even the road to school all stand on land — and India cannot make more of it!
p: Land supports natural vegetation, wildlife, human life, economic activities, transport and communication. It is a limited asset, and about 95% of our basic needs for food, shelter and clothing come from land.

India's land: about 43% plains (good for farming and industry), about 30% mountains (source of perennial rivers, tourism and ecological balance) and about 27% plateaus (rich in minerals, fossil fuels and forests).

Land use categories: forests; land not available for cultivation (barren and wasteland, land for non-agricultural uses); other uncultivated land (pastures, tree crops and groves, culturable waste land); fallow land; and net sown area. Gross cropped area = net sown area + area sown more than once in a year.
Fallow land: current fallow is left uncultivated for one year or less; other than current fallow for 1 to 5 years. Culturable waste land is left uncultivated for more than 5 agricultural years.

Land degradation is caused by mining and deforestation (Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha), overgrazing (Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra) and over-irrigation that causes waterlogging, salinity and alkalinity (Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh). Remedies include afforestation, controlled grazing, shelter belts, thorny bushes on sand dunes and treating industrial waste.

ex.q: A farmer in Punjab sowed wheat in winter and rice in the rainy season on the same 10 hectares. A neighbour sowed only one crop on his 6 hectares. Together, what is their net sown area and gross cropped area?
st: Net sown area counts each field once: 10 + 6 = 16 hectares.
Gross cropped area adds the area sown more than once: the first farmer's 10 hectares were sown twice, so add 10 more.
Gross cropped area = 16 + 10 = 26 hectares.
ex.a: Net sown area 16 hectares; gross cropped area 26 hectares.

topics.rl: On a train ride through Punjab you see fields almost everywhere — over 80% of its area is net sown — while in Arunachal Pradesh you see mostly forested hills.

topics.t: Soils of India and soil conservation
topics.h: It can take millions of years for nature to make just a few centimetres of soil — and a single heavy rain can wash it away!
p: Soil is the most important renewable natural resource. Relief, parent rock, climate, vegetation, other life forms and time decide which soil forms.

Alluvial soil, the most widespread, was deposited by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra and covers the northern plains and the eastern coastal deltas. Old alluvium is bangar (more kankar nodules); new alluvium is khadar (finer and more fertile). It is rich in potash, phosphoric acid and lime, good for sugarcane, paddy and wheat.

Black soil (regur or black cotton soil) formed from Deccan trap lava and is found in Maharashtra, Saurashtra, Malwa, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh. It holds moisture, is rich in calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime but poor in phosphoric content, develops deep cracks in summer and is sticky when wet.

Red and yellow soil forms on crystalline igneous and metamorphic rocks; iron makes it red, and it looks yellow when hydrated. Laterite soil (from the Latin 'later', brick) forms under high temperature and heavy rain with intense leaching; with care it grows tea and coffee, and red laterite in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Kerala suits cashew. Arid soil is sandy and saline with a kankar layer below; forest soils are found in hilly areas and are acidic with little humus in snowy regions.

Soil erosion: running water cuts gullies and makes 'bad land' (ravines in the Chambal basin); sheet erosion washes away topsoil; wind blows loose soil away; ploughing up and down slopes speeds it up. Conservation: contour ploughing, terrace farming (western and central Himalayas), strip cropping (grass strips break the wind) and shelter belts of trees (which have stabilised sand dunes in western India).

ex.q: A farmer on a hill slope in Uttarakhand sees that rain washes his soil downhill every monsoon. What should he do and why?
st: Rain water rushes straight down a steep slope and carries soil with it.
Cutting steps (terraces) on the slope makes flat strips that slow the water down.
Ploughing along the contour lines instead of up and down also stops water from forming channels.
ex.a: Use terrace farming and contour ploughing so water slows down and the soil stays.

topics.rl: Cotton farmers of Vidarbha in Maharashtra grow cotton on black soil, which holds moisture well — that is why it is called black cotton soil.

topics.t: Biodiversity and the need for conservation
topics.h: From tiny lichens on a rock to a huge banyan tree and a blue whale — every living thing is a thread in one giant web, and we are part of it too!
p: Biodiversity means the variety of life on Earth — micro-organisms, bacteria and lichens, plants like the banyan, and animals like elephants and blue whales. India is one of the world's richest countries in biological diversity.
Humans are part of this web of life. Plants, animals and micro-organisms keep the air we breathe, the water we drink and the soil that grows our food healthy.
Forests are primary producers: all other living beings depend on them for food and shelter.

Conservation preserves ecological diversity and our life-support systems (water, air and soil). It also protects the genetic diversity of plants and animals, which helps species grow and breed — agriculture and fisheries depend on it.

The Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act was implemented in 1972: it banned hunting, gave legal protection to habitats and restricted trade in wildlife. National parks and wildlife sanctuaries were set up, and special projects protected animals such as the one-horned rhinoceros, hangul (Kashmir stag), gharial and Asiatic lion.

ex.q: Bees disappear from an area because of heavy pesticide use. Why should a mango farmer nearby worry?
st: Bees carry pollen from flower to flower — they pollinate crops.
Without pollination, many mango flowers will not turn into fruit.
So losing one small insect species can reduce the farmer's harvest; every species is linked in the web of life.
ex.a: Because pollinators like bees are needed for fruit to form; losing them hurts farming.

topics.rl: When you visit Kaziranga in Assam and see a one-horned rhinoceros, you are seeing a species that survived because of conservation laws and protected areas.

topics.t: Project Tiger and types of forests
topics.h: In 1973 India's tiger count had fallen to 1,827. A special project was launched to bring the striped king back!
p: Project Tiger was launched in 1973. According to the textbook, India's tiger population had fallen from an estimated 55,000 at the turn of the twentieth century to 1,827 in 1973.
Major threats to tigers: poaching for trade, shrinking habitat, depletion of prey species and a growing human population.

Some tiger reserves: Corbett National Park (Uttarakhand), Sundarbans National Park (West Bengal), Bandhavgarh National Park (Madhya Pradesh), Sariska Wildlife Sanctuary (Rajasthan), Manas Tiger Reserve (Assam) and Periyar Tiger Reserve (Kerala).

Reserved forests make up more than half of India's forest land and are the most valuable for conserving forests and wildlife. Protected forests are about one-third and are protected from further depletion. Unclassed forests are other forests and wastelands owned by the government, private individuals and communities.

Reserved and protected forests are permanent forest estates. Madhya Pradesh has the largest area under permanent forests. The north-eastern states and parts of Gujarat have a high share of unclassed forests managed by local communities.

ex.q: Saving tigers also saves many other plants and animals. How?
st: A tiger needs a large, healthy forest with plenty of deer and other prey.
To protect tigers, the whole forest, its grasslands and water sources must be protected.
So every other species living there — birds, insects, plants — is protected too. The tiger is like an umbrella for the ecosystem.
ex.a: Protecting a tiger means protecting its whole habitat and food chain, so many species benefit.

topics.rl: Families visiting Corbett in Uttarakhand or Periyar in Kerala support conservation by following park rules — no plastic, no noise and no feeding animals.

topics.h: Long before laws were written, villagers in India were protecting trees and animals as if they were family!
p: In Sariska Tiger Reserve (Rajasthan), villagers fought against mining by citing the Wildlife Protection Act.
In Alwar district (Rajasthan), five villages declared about 1,200 hectares of forest as the Bhairodev Dakav 'Sonchuri', with their own rules that ban hunting and protect wildlife from outsiders.

The Chipko movement in the Himalayas resisted deforestation and showed that community afforestation with local species can succeed. The Beej Bachao Andolan in Tehri and Navdanya showed that diverse crops can be grown without synthetic chemicals.

Joint Forest Management (JFM) involves local communities in managing and restoring degraded forests. It began in 1988 when Odisha passed the first resolution; in return, villagers get non-timber forest produce and a share of timber.

Sacred groves are forest patches protected because of local beliefs. The Mundas and Santhals of Chota Nagpur worship mahua and kadamba trees; tribals of Odisha and Bihar worship tamarind and mango trees during weddings; peepal and banyan are considered sacred by many. In Bishnoi villages of Rajasthan, blackbuck, nilgai and peacocks live safely as part of the community.

ex.q: Why does Joint Forest Management work better than just putting a fence around a degraded forest?
st: Local people live near the forest and know it best.
Under JFM they protect it, and in return they get non-timber forest produce and a share of the timber.
Because they benefit, they have a reason to guard the forest every day.
ex.a: JFM gives local communities both responsibility and benefits, so they protect the forest themselves.

topics.rl: When your family ties a thread around a peepal tree or protects an old banyan near a temple, it is part of a long Indian tradition that also conserves nature.

topics.t: Water scarcity and the need for conservation
topics.h: Water is renewable — the water cycle keeps refilling it — so why do so many Indian towns queue up for tankers every summer?
p: Fresh water is renewed by the hydrological (water) cycle, yet many regions face water scarcity.
Scarcity is often caused not by low rainfall alone but by over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access to water among different social groups.
A growing population needs more food, so more land is irrigated, even in the dry season; heavy pumping of groundwater through wells and tube wells lowers the water table.
Industries need water and also power, much of which comes from hydroelectricity. Growing cities make things worse — many housing societies pump their own groundwater.
Even where there is plenty of water, it may be unfit to use because of domestic and industrial waste, chemicals, pesticides and fertilisers — this also causes scarcity.

ex.q: A city gets good rainfall, yet many families buy drinking water. Give two possible reasons.
st: Check quantity: is there enough water? Rainfall is good, so quantity may not be the problem.
Check quality: sewage or factory waste may have polluted the local river or lake.
Check access: groundwater may be over-pumped or unequally shared, so some areas get too little.
ex.a: Water pollution and over-use or unequal access can cause scarcity even where rainfall is good.

topics.rl: Turning off the tap while brushing your teeth and reusing RO waste water to mop the floor are small ways your family can fight water scarcity.

topics.h: One dam, many jobs: it can water fields, light homes, stop floods and even grow fish!
p: A dam is a barrier across flowing water that blocks or slows the flow, often creating a reservoir. Multipurpose projects use it for irrigation, electricity, water supply, flood control, recreation, inland navigation and fish breeding.
Jawaharlal Nehru proudly called dams the 'temples of modern India' because they would link agriculture with industrial growth.
Examples: Bhakra Nangal (Sutlej-Beas basin) is used for hydel power and irrigation; Hirakud on the Mahanadi combines water conservation with flood control.

Problems: dams disrupt a river's natural flow, cause sedimentation in reservoirs, affect aquatic life and fish migration, submerge forests and soil, and displace local communities. Over-irrigation can cause salinisation of soil, and sharing of water can lead to inter-state disputes.
Movements such as the Narmada Bachao Andolan (about the Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada) and the Tehri Dam Andolan raised concerns about displaced people and the environment.

ex.q: A dam was built to control floods, yet the area downstream flooded badly after very heavy rain. How can this happen?
st: Over the years, sediment settles in the reservoir and reduces how much water it can hold.
During extreme rain the reservoir fills quickly, and water must be released.
Large releases from the dam can flood the area downstream.
ex.a: Sedimentation reduces storage, and excess water released during heavy rain can cause floods.

topics.rl: The electricity that runs the fans in many homes of Punjab and Himachal Pradesh comes partly from hydel projects like Bhakra Nangal.

topics.h: In the Thar desert, families once stored every drop of rain under their homes in tanks as big as rooms — and called it 'palar pani'!
p: Rainwater harvesting means collecting and storing rainwater for later use. Traditional Indian methods are cheap, eco-friendly and suited to local conditions.
In hilly regions of the western Himalayas, people built diversion channels called 'guls' or 'kuls' for farming. In the floodplains of Bengal, people built inundation channels to irrigate fields.
In arid and semi-arid Rajasthan, fields were turned into rain-fed storage structures, such as 'khadins' in Jaisalmer and 'johads' in other areas, to keep the soil moist.

In Bikaner, Phalodi and Barmer (Rajasthan), rooftop rainwater was piped into underground 'tankas'. The first spell of rain was not collected, to clean the roof and pipes. This stored water, called 'palar pani', was considered the purest form of natural water, and rooms built next to tankas stayed cool in summer.

Today: Tamil Nadu was the first state to make rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for all houses; Gendathur village in Karnataka harvests rooftop rainwater in about 200 households; Shillong in Meghalaya meets part of its household needs this way; and Meghalaya has a 200-year-old system of bamboo drip irrigation.

ex.q: Why did families in Rajasthan let the first rain of the season flow away instead of storing it in the tanka?
st: The first rain washes dust, leaves and bird droppings off the roof and pipes.
If that water entered the tanka, the stored drinking water would become dirty.
So the first spell was let go, and the cleaner rain that followed was stored.
ex.a: The first rain cleans the roof and pipes, so only the cleaner later rain is stored.

topics.rl: Many apartment buildings in Chennai and Bengaluru now have rooftop pipes leading rain into recharge pits — a modern version of the old tanka idea.

topics.h: Some farmers in the north-east burn a patch of forest, farm it for a few years and move on — while a Punjab farmer uses tractors, tube wells and HYV seeds on the same field every year!
p: Primitive subsistence farming is done on small patches with simple tools like the hoe, dao and digging sticks, using family or community labour. It depends on the monsoon and the natural fertility of the soil.

In slash and burn ('shifting') agriculture, farmers clear a patch of forest, grow food crops, and move to a fresh patch when the soil loses fertility. It is called jhumming in the north-eastern states, bewar or dahiya in Madhya Pradesh, podu or penda in Andhra Pradesh, valre or waltre in south-eastern Rajasthan and khil in the Himalayan belt; abroad it is milpa in Mexico and Central America and roca in Brazil.

Intensive subsistence farming is practised where there is high population pressure on land. It is labour-intensive and uses high doses of biochemical inputs and irrigation. Land divided among heirs over generations has made many holdings too small to be economical.

Commercial farming uses modern inputs such as high yielding variety (HYV) seeds, chemical fertilisers, insecticides and pesticides to get higher productivity. The same crop can be commercial in one place and subsistence in another — rice is commercial in Punjab and Haryana but subsistence in Odisha.

Plantation farming grows a single crop on a large area, using capital and migrant labour, and produce is used as raw material in industries. Examples: tea, coffee, rubber, sugarcane and banana. Tea is grown in Assam and North Bengal, coffee in Karnataka.

ex.q: A tea estate in Assam covers hundreds of hectares, employs many workers and sends its leaves to a factory on the estate. What type of farming is this, and why?
st: Only one crop (tea) is grown over a large area — a feature of plantations.
It needs a lot of capital and labour.
Its produce is raw material for an industry (tea processing), and it is grown for sale.
ex.a: Plantation farming — a single commercial crop on a large estate linked to processing industry.

topics.rl: The banana chips and the cup of Assam tea at your breakfast both come from plantation farming.

topics.h: India has not one but three crop seasons — that is why your mandi has fresh peas in winter and watermelons in summer!
p: India has three main cropping seasons: rabi, kharif and zaid.

Rabi crops are sown in winter (October to December) and harvested in summer (April to June). Examples: wheat, barley, peas, gram and mustard. Winter rain from western temperate cyclones helps these crops in the north.
Kharif crops are sown with the onset of the monsoon and harvested in September–October. Examples: paddy (rice), maize, jowar, bajra, tur (arhar), moong, urad, cotton, jute, groundnut and soyabean.
Zaid is a short season in summer between the rabi and kharif seasons. Examples: watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables and fodder crops. Sugarcane takes almost a year to grow.
In Assam, West Bengal and Odisha, three crops of paddy are grown in a year: aus, aman and boro.

ex.q: A farmer in Haryana harvests wheat in April. Which season's crop is this, and what could he grow on the same field in June–July?
st: Wheat is sown in winter and harvested in April–June, so it is a rabi crop.
In June–July the monsoon arrives, which is when kharif crops are sown.
So he could sow a kharif crop such as paddy (if irrigated) or bajra.
ex.a: Wheat is a rabi crop; in June–July he can sow a kharif crop like rice or bajra.

topics.rl: Juicy watermelons and cucumbers piled up at fruit stalls in May are zaid crops, grown in the short summer season.

topics.h: Your plate of rice, roti, bajra bhakri and dal comes from four very different kinds of crops — each with its own favourite weather!
p: Rice is a kharif crop that needs high temperature (above 25°C), high humidity and annual rainfall above 100 cm; in drier areas it grows with irrigation. Canals and tube wells allow rice in Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan.

Wheat is the main rabi food crop of north and north-west India. It needs a cool growing season, bright sunshine at ripening and 50 to 75 cm of rainfall spread over the growing season. Its two main zones are the Ganga-Satluj plains in the north-west and the black soil region of the Deccan.

Jowar, bajra and ragi are millets ('coarse grains') with very high nutritional value. Jowar is the third most important food crop by area and production and is mostly rain-fed. Bajra grows well on sandy and shallow black soils. Ragi grows in dry regions and is very rich in iron, calcium and other micro-nutrients.
Maize is used for both food and fodder. It is a kharif crop needing 21°C to 27°C and grows well in old alluvial soil; in Bihar it is also grown in the rabi season.

Pulses such as tur (arhar), urad, moong, masur, peas and gram need little moisture and survive in dry conditions. Being leguminous crops, they help restore soil fertility by fixing nitrogen from the air, so they are grown in rotation with other crops.

ex.q: A farmer in Madhya Pradesh grows wheat every year and finds his soil becoming less fertile. Which crop could he rotate with wheat to help the soil, and why?
st: Wheat takes nitrogen out of the soil.
Leguminous pulses like gram or moong have root nodules that fix nitrogen from the air.
Growing pulses in rotation adds nitrogen back, so the soil regains fertility.
ex.a: A leguminous pulse such as gram, because it fixes atmospheric nitrogen and restores soil fertility.

topics.rl: Ragi dosa and ragi malt are popular in Karnataka because ragi is rich in iron and calcium — a millet that is great for growing teenagers.

topics.h: Your morning chai, the cotton of your school uniform, the rubber of your eraser and the jute bag at the sabzi market all grow on Indian farms!
p: Sugarcane is a tropical and subtropical crop needing a hot, humid climate (21°C to 27°C) and 75 to 100 cm of rainfall; irrigation is needed where rain is low. It is the main source of sugar, gur (jaggery), khandsari and molasses, and it needs manual labour from sowing to harvesting.
Oilseeds: groundnut is a kharif crop; mustard and linseed are rabi crops; sesamum is kharif in the north and rabi in the south; castor seed is grown as both rabi and kharif.

Tea was introduced in India by the British. It needs a warm, moist, frost-free climate, deep fertile well-drained soil rich in humus, and frequent showers spread through the year; it is labour-intensive. Coffee in India is mainly the Arabica variety, first brought from Yemen and first grown on the Baba Budan Hills; it is grown in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

Rubber is an equatorial crop that also grows in tropical areas under special conditions: rainfall above 200 cm and temperature above 25°C. It is grown in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and the Garo Hills of Meghalaya.

Cotton grows well in the drier parts of the black cotton soil of the Deccan; it needs high temperature, light rainfall or irrigation, 210 frost-free days and bright sunshine, and takes 6 to 8 months to mature. Jute, the 'golden fibre', grows on well-drained fertile soils of flood plains renewed every year (West Bengal, Bihar, Assam, Odisha, Meghalaya). Horticulture includes famous fruits like Nagpur oranges and the apples of Jammu and Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh.

ex.q: Why is jute grown mainly in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta region of West Bengal rather than in Rajasthan?
st: Jute needs high temperature during its growth.
It needs well-drained, fertile soil of flood plains, which is renewed every year by river floods.
The delta of West Bengal has both; Rajasthan is dry and has no such flood plains.
ex.a: Because jute needs hot weather and fertile flood-plain soil renewed each year, found in West Bengal's delta, not in dry Rajasthan.

topics.rl: Jute bags that replace plastic carry bags at many shops come from the 'golden fibre' grown in West Bengal and Assam.

topics.h: Your toothpaste, the steel spoon in your tiffin and even the salt on your chips all contain minerals dug out of the Earth!
p: A mineral is a homogeneous, naturally occurring substance with a definable internal structure. Minerals are found in rocks; an ore is an accumulation of a mineral mixed with other elements, in high enough concentration to be mined profitably.

Types of minerals: metallic — ferrous (iron ore and the minerals used with it to make iron and steel, such as manganese, nickel and cobalt), non-ferrous (copper, lead, tin, bauxite) and precious (gold, silver, platinum); non-metallic (mica, salt, potash, sulphur, granite, limestone, marble, sandstone); and energy minerals (coal, petroleum, natural gas).

Occurrence: in veins and lodes in igneous and metamorphic rocks (tin, copper, zinc, lead); in beds or layers of sedimentary rocks (coal, some iron ore, gypsum, potash salt, sodium salt); from decomposition of surface rocks (bauxite); as placer deposits in the sands of valley floors and hill bases (gold, silver, tin, platinum); and in ocean waters (common salt, magnesium, bromine) with manganese nodules on the ocean floor.
Rat-hole mining, done in narrow tunnels by families in Jowai and Cherapunjee (Meghalaya), has been declared illegal by the National Green Tribunal.
Minerals are finite and non-renewable — they take millions of years to form. We must conserve them by recycling metals, using scrap metal and finding substitutes.

ex.q: Gold is sometimes found in the sands of riverbeds far from any gold mine. How?
st: Gold exists in rocks on hills upstream.
Running water slowly wears away these rocks; gold is not corroded by water.
Heavy gold particles settle in the sands of valley floors and the base of hills — these are placer deposits.
ex.a: Gold settles as placer deposits in river sands after being washed out of rocks upstream.

topics.rl: Aluminium cans and old steel utensils sent to the kabadiwala are recycled into new metal, saving minerals that took millions of years to form.

topics.t: Important minerals and where they are found
topics.h: The Bailadila hills of Chhattisgarh got their name because they look like the hump of an ox — and they are full of high-grade iron ore!
p: Iron ore is the basic mineral and backbone of industrial development. Magnetite is the finest ore (up to 70% iron) with excellent magnetic qualities; hematite is the most important industrial ore by quantity used (50–60% iron).

Iron ore belts: Odisha–Jharkhand (Badampahar in Odisha; Gua and Noamundi in Jharkhand); Durg–Bastar–Chandrapur (Bailadila hills, exported through Visakhapatnam port); Ballari–Chitradurga–Chikkamagaluru–Tumakuru in Karnataka (Kudremukh, a 100% export unit, sends ore as slurry by pipeline to a port near Mangaluru); and Maharashtra–Goa (exported through Marmagao port).
Manganese is mainly used in making steel and ferro-manganese alloy — nearly 10 kg of manganese is needed for one tonne of steel. It is also used in bleaching powder, insecticides and paints.

Copper (good conductor, used in electric cables): Balaghat (Madhya Pradesh), Khetri (Rajasthan), Singhbhum (Jharkhand). Bauxite (for aluminium): Amarkantak plateau, Maikal hills and Bilaspur–Katni plateau; Panchpatmali in Koraput (Odisha). Mica (insulator for electrical and electronic goods): Koderma–Gaya–Hazaribagh belt (Jharkhand), Ajmer, Nellore. Limestone is the basic raw material for cement and is used in smelting iron ore.
Mining hazards: dust and harmful fumes cause lung diseases in miners; mines risk roof collapse, flooding and fire; waste and slurry pollute land, soil, streams and rivers.

ex.q: Why is mica so useful in the electronics industry?
st: Mica can be split into very thin sheets.
It has excellent di-electric strength, low power loss and resists high voltage — it insulates well.
So it is used to insulate parts in electrical and electronic equipment.
ex.a: Because mica splits into thin sheets and is an excellent insulator that resists high voltage.

topics.rl: The cement in your school building is made from limestone, and the copper wires in your home wiring may come from mines like Khetri or Balaghat.

topics.h: The light in your room may come from coal that began as a swamp forest about 200 million years ago!
p: Conventional sources of energy: firewood, cattle dung cake, coal, petroleum, natural gas and electricity (hydel and thermal). Burning dung cake is being discouraged because it uses up valuable manure.

Coal forms by compression of plant material over millions of years. Grades by rising quality: peat, lignite (low-grade brown coal with high moisture; main reserves at Neyveli, Tamil Nadu), bituminous (most popular for commercial use; metallurgical coal for smelting iron) and anthracite (highest quality hard coal).

Gondwana coal is about 200 million years old and is found mainly in the Damodar valley (Jharia, Raniganj and Bokaro). Tertiary coal is about 55 million years old and occurs in Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland. Coal is bulky, so heavy industries and thermal power stations are located near coalfields.

Petroleum gives fuel for heat and lighting, lubricants and raw materials; refineries are a 'nodal industry' for synthetic textiles, fertilisers and chemicals. Main areas: Mumbai High, Gujarat (Ankleshwar is the most important field) and Assam, the oldest oil-producing state (Digboi, Naharkatiya, Moran-Hugrijan).

Natural gas is a clean fuel (CNG for vehicles) and petrochemical raw material, found in the Krishna-Godavari basin, Mumbai High, the Gulf of Khambhat and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. The 1,700 km Hazira–Vijaipur–Jagdishpur (HVJ) pipeline carries it to western and northern India. Hydel power uses fast-flowing water (renewable); thermal power burns coal, petroleum or natural gas (non-renewable).

ex.q: Why are steel plants and thermal power stations usually built on or near coalfields?
st: Coal is bulky and heavy, so transporting it is costly.
When coal is burnt, it loses weight and turns to ash.
Building the plant near the coalfield saves the cost of carrying large amounts of coal.
ex.a: Because coal is a bulky material that loses weight on burning, so it is cheaper to use it near where it is mined.

topics.rl: Many autos and buses in Delhi run on CNG, a cleaner fuel made from natural gas.

topics.h: The sun, the wind, the tides, the Earth's inner heat and even cow dung can light up India — without running out!
p: Non-conventional sources: solar, wind, tidal, geothermal, biogas and nuclear (atomic) energy. They are needed because fossil fuels are limited and cause pollution.

Nuclear energy is obtained by altering the structure of atoms, which releases heat used to make electricity. Uranium and thorium are found in Jharkhand and the Aravalli ranges of Rajasthan; the monazite sands of Kerala are rich in thorium.

Solar energy: India is a tropical country, and photovoltaic technology converts sunlight directly into electricity. Wind energy: the textbook describes the cluster from Nagercoil to Madurai in Tamil Nadu as India's largest wind farm cluster; Nagercoil and Jaisalmer are well known for using wind energy effectively.

Biogas is made from shrubs, farm waste and animal and human waste; it has higher thermal efficiency than kerosene, dung cake and charcoal. 'Gobar gas' plants give two benefits: energy and better-quality manure. Tidal energy: the Gulf of Khambhat and Gulf of Kachchh (Gujarat) and the Sundarbans (West Bengal) have ideal conditions. Geothermal energy: experimental projects at Parvati valley near Manikarn (Himachal Pradesh) and Puga valley (Ladakh).
Conserving energy: 'energy saved is energy produced'. Use public transport, switch off lights and fans when not in use, use power-saving devices and use non-conventional sources.

ex.q: A village has many cattle and the families cook with dung cakes. Why would a gobar gas plant be better?
st: Burning dung cakes is smoky and wastes dung that could be manure.
In a gobar gas plant, dung decomposes to give biogas, a cleaner fuel with higher thermal efficiency.
The slurry left behind is excellent manure for the fields — so the village gets both energy and manure.
ex.a: It gives cleaner, more efficient fuel and also good manure — twin benefits.

topics.rl: Rooftop solar panels on homes and schools across India use photovoltaic cells to turn sunlight directly into electricity.

topics.t: Importance, location and classification of industries
topics.h: Raw cotton is worth a little; the same cotton turned into a school shirt is worth much more. Manufacturing is the magic of adding value!
p: Manufacturing means producing goods in large quantities after processing raw materials into more valuable products. It is the backbone of development: it modernises agriculture, reduces dependence on farm income by creating jobs in the secondary and tertiary sectors, helps remove unemployment and poverty, and earns foreign exchange through exports.
Agriculture and industry go hand in hand: agro-industries raise farm productivity, and industries sell farmers things like irrigation pumps, fertilisers, pesticides, PVC pipes, machines and tools.

Industrial location depends on raw material, labour, capital, power and market. Many industries cluster in cities to use shared services such as banking, insurance, transport, labour and consultants — these advantages are called agglomeration economies.

Industries are classified by source of raw material (agro-based, mineral-based), main role (basic or key industries like iron and steel that supply others; consumer industries like sugar, toothpaste, paper and sewing machines), capital investment (small scale or large scale), ownership and bulk and weight of raw materials and finished goods (heavy like iron and steel; light like electrical goods).

By ownership: public sector (run by the government, e.g. BHEL, SAIL); private sector (owned by individuals or groups, e.g. TISCO, Bajaj Auto, Dabur); joint sector (run jointly by the state and individuals, e.g. Oil India Ltd); cooperative sector (owned by producers or workers, e.g. sugar industry in Maharashtra and coir industry in Kerala).

ex.q: A new textile mill owner must choose between a remote village and the outskirts of a big city. Why might the city be a better choice?
st: The city offers a big market for finished cloth.
It has banks, insurance, transport links and skilled labour already available.
Being near other industries lets the mill share these services — agglomeration economies.
ex.a: The city, because it offers markets and shared services — the advantages of agglomeration economies.

topics.rl: In Tiruppur (Tamil Nadu) or Ludhiana (Punjab), many garment and hosiery units cluster together to share workers, suppliers and transport — agglomeration economies in action.

topics.h: The cotton in your kurta, the jute in a gunny bag and the sugar in your kheer all travelled from a farm to a factory first!
p: Agro-based industries use plant and animal products as raw materials: cotton, wool, jute, silk textiles, rubber, sugar, tea, coffee and edible oil industries.
The textile industry is the only industry in India that is self-reliant and complete in the value chain — from raw material to the highest value-added products.

The first successful textile mill was set up in Mumbai in 1854. Early mills grew in the cotton belt of Maharashtra and Gujarat because of raw cotton, markets, transport and ports, labour and a moist climate. Spinning is centralised in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Tamil Nadu, while weaving is highly decentralised (handloom, powerloom and mills); khadi gives home-based employment to weavers.

The first jute mill was set up near Kolkata at Rishra in 1855. Jute mills are mostly located along the banks of the Hugli river because of nearby jute-growing areas, cheap water transport, good railway and road links, abundant water for processing, cheap labour and Kolkata's banking, insurance and port facilities.
Sugar is another major agro-based industry; many sugar mills in Maharashtra are run as cooperatives owned by cane farmers.

ex.q: Why did jute mills come up along the Hugli river and not near Mumbai?
st: Raw jute is grown in West Bengal and nearby areas, close to the Hugli.
The river gives cheap water transport and the abundant water needed to process jute.
Kolkata nearby provides labour, banking, insurance and a port for exports.
ex.a: Because the Hugli belt is close to jute fields and offers water, cheap transport, labour and Kolkata's port and services.

topics.rl: A hand-woven khadi kurta or a Chanderi or Kanchipuram saree comes from the decentralised weaving sector that supports lakhs of weaver families.

topics.h: Every bridge, bus and bicycle begins in a fiery blast furnace that turns iron ore into steel!
p: Mineral-based industries use minerals and metals as raw materials: iron and steel, cement, aluminium, machine tools and petrochemicals.

Iron and steel is the basic industry — all other industries, heavy, medium and light, depend on it for machinery. It is a heavy industry because its raw materials and finished goods are bulky. Iron ore, coking coal and limestone are needed in a ratio of about 4:2:1, with some manganese to harden the steel.
The Chhotanagpur plateau has the maximum concentration of iron and steel industries because of low-cost iron ore, high-grade raw materials close by, cheap labour and a large home market.

Aluminium smelting is the second most important metallurgical industry in India. Aluminium is light, resists corrosion, conducts heat well and is malleable; it is used in aircraft, utensils and wires. Bauxite is its raw material, and smelters need a regular supply of electricity and raw material at minimum cost.

The chemical industry has inorganic chemicals (sulphuric acid, nitric acid, soda ash, caustic soda) and organic chemicals (petrochemicals); it is its own largest consumer. The fertiliser industry makes nitrogenous (mainly urea), phosphatic and complex fertilisers; potash is entirely imported. Cement needs bulky limestone, silica and gypsum. Bengaluru is called the electronic capital of India.

ex.q: Why is the iron and steel industry called both a 'basic' industry and a 'heavy' industry?
st: Basic: other industries depend on steel to make their machinery.
Heavy: its raw materials (iron ore, coal, limestone) and products (steel) are bulky and heavy.
So the name 'basic' comes from its role and 'heavy' from the weight of its materials.
ex.a: Basic because other industries need its products for machinery; heavy because its raw materials and finished goods are bulky.

topics.rl: The pressure cooker and the window frames in your home are probably made of aluminium — light, rust-free and a good conductor of heat.

topics.h: Factories make the things we love, but they can also make the air smoky, rivers dirty and cities noisy — unless we control them!
p: Industries cause four types of pollution: air, water, land and noise.

Air pollution comes from gases like sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide and from particulate matter (dust, smoke, mist) released by factories, refineries, smelting plants, brick kilns and the burning of fossil fuels.

Water pollution comes from industrial effluents containing dyes, detergents, acids, salts and heavy metals like lead and mercury (from paper, chemical, textile and dyeing industries, refineries, tanneries and electroplating units). Thermal pollution happens when hot water from factories and thermal plants is drained into rivers and ponds before cooling. Fly ash, phosphogypsum and iron and steel slag are major solid wastes.

Land pollution happens when waste and chemicals are dumped on soil; rainwater can carry these pollutants down to groundwater. Noise from machinery, generators and drills causes irritation, hearing loss and raised heart rate and blood pressure.

Control: reuse and recycle water; harvest rainwater; treat effluents in three stages — primary (mechanical: screening, grinding, flocculation, sedimentation), secondary (biological) and tertiary (biological, chemical and physical, with recycling); fit smoke stacks with electrostatic precipitators, fabric filters, scrubbers and inertial separators; use oil or gas instead of coal; fit generators with silencers and use noise-absorbing material and ear plugs. NTPC has ISO 14001 certification and uses ash utilisation, green belts and ash-water recycling.

ex.q: A dyeing unit in a textile town wants to stop polluting the nearby river. Suggest steps in the right order.
st: First, reduce water use by reusing and recycling it in successive stages.
Then treat the effluent: primary (mechanical — screening and settling), secondary (biological) and tertiary (chemical, physical and biological, with recycling).
Release only cooled, treated water — never hot or untreated water.
ex.a: Reuse water, treat effluents in primary, secondary and tertiary stages, and release only cooled, treated water.

topics.rl: When you see a tall factory chimney with little visible smoke, it is probably fitted with an electrostatic precipitator that traps dust before it reaches your lungs.

topics.h: A truck carrying Nashik onions can drive straight from the farm to your local mandi — no station, no port. That is the power of roads!
p: Roads have advantages over railways: they cost less to build, can cross dissected and undulating land and high mountains like the Himalayas, are economical for a few people and small loads over short distances, give door-to-door service and act as feeders to railways, ports and airports.

The Golden Quadrilateral super highways are six-lane roads linking Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Mumbai. The North-South corridor links Srinagar with Kanniyakumari, and the East-West corridor links Silchar (Assam) with Porbandar (Gujarat). They aim to reduce the time and distance between mega cities and are implemented by the National Highway Authority of India (NHAI).

National highways link the extreme parts of the country and form the primary road system. State highways link a state capital with district headquarters and are built and maintained by the State Public Works Department (PWD). District roads connect district headquarters with other places and are maintained by the Zila Parishad.

Other roads (rural roads) link villages with towns; they received a special boost under the Pradhan Mantri Grameen Sadak Yojana. Border roads are built and maintained by the Border Roads Organisation (established in 1960) in strategic northern and north-eastern border areas.

By material, roads are metalled (made of cement, concrete or bitumen — all-weather roads) or unmetalled (may become unusable in the rainy season). Road density is the length of roads per 100 sq km of area.

ex.q: A family wants to send a small parcel of homemade pickles from Jaipur to a village 60 km away. Is road or rail better, and why?
st: The distance is short and the load is small.
Roads give door-to-door service and lower loading and unloading costs.
A train would need trips to and from stations at both ends.
ex.a: Road — it is cheaper and gives door-to-door service for small loads over short distances.

topics.rl: When your bus zooms along a six-lane expressway between Delhi and Kolkata, you may be on a stretch of the Golden Quadrilateral.

topics.h: India's first passenger train in 1853 chugged just 34 km — today trains carry crores of people across the whole country!
p: Railways are the principal mode of transport for freight and passengers in India and help business, sightseeing and pilgrimage. The first train ran from Mumbai to Thane in 1853, covering 34 km.

Relief affects railways: the level northern plains with dense population and rich agriculture are ideal; the Himalayas and hilly areas, deserts of Rajasthan, swamps of Gujarat and thick forests are difficult. The Konkan Railway along the west coast faced problems like sinking tracks and landslides.

Pipelines carry water, crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas to refineries, fertiliser factories and big thermal power plants; solids can move as slurry. Building them is costly, but running costs are minimal and there are no trans-shipment losses or delays. Main networks: Upper Assam to Kanpur (Uttar Pradesh); Salaya (Gujarat) to Jalandhar (Punjab); and the gas pipeline from Hazira (Gujarat) via Vijaipur (Madhya Pradesh) to Jagdishpur (Uttar Pradesh).
Waterways are the cheapest means of transport, fuel-efficient and environment-friendly, and are most suitable for heavy and bulky goods.

National Waterway No. 1: the Ganga between Prayagraj (Allahabad) and Haldia (1,620 km). National Waterway No. 2: the Brahmaputra between Sadiya and Dhubri (891 km). National Waterway No. 3: the West Coast Canal in Kerala (Kottapuram–Kollam, Udyogamandal and Champakkara canals — 205 km).

ex.q: Why is it easier to build railway lines in the Ganga plains than in Arunachal Pradesh?
st: The Ganga plains are vast and level; Arunachal Pradesh is mountainous with steep slopes.
Plains need no tunnels or steep bridges, so building is cheaper.
Dense population and rich agriculture in the plains also mean more passengers and goods.
ex.a: The plains are level, densely populated and agriculturally rich, while the mountains are steep and difficult to build on.

topics.rl: The petrol filled in your family scooter may have reached a nearby depot through an underground pipeline, without a single truck trip.

topics.h: Mumbai, Visakhapatnam, Kochi — India's ports are giant doorways where ships carry our goods to the world!
p: Most of India's foreign trade by volume moves through its sea ports. Major ports on the west coast: Kandla (Deendayal Port), Mumbai, Jawaharlal Nehru Port, Marmagao, New Mangalore and Kochi. On the east coast: Tuticorin (V.O. Chidambaranar), Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Paradip, Kolkata and Haldia.

Kandla in Kachchh was the first port developed after Independence, to ease the load on Mumbai port after Karachi went to Pakistan at Partition; it is a tidal port. Mumbai is the biggest port, with a spacious natural and well-sheltered harbour; Jawaharlal Nehru Port was planned to decongest it.

Marmagao (Goa) is the premier iron ore exporting port. New Mangalore (Karnataka) exports iron ore concentrates from the Kudremukh mines. Kochi is the extreme south-western port, at the entrance of a lagoon with a natural harbour. Tuticorin (Tamil Nadu) has a natural harbour and trades with Sri Lanka and the Maldives.

Chennai is one of the oldest artificial ports. Visakhapatnam is the deepest landlocked and well-protected port. Paradip (Odisha) specialises in iron ore exports. Kolkata is an inland riverine port on the Hugli that needs constant dredging; Haldia was developed as a subsidiary port to relieve pressure on Kolkata.

Airways are the fastest, most comfortable and prestigious mode of transport and can cross high mountains, deserts, dense forests and long ocean stretches. Pawan Hans Helicopters Ltd provides helicopter services to ONGC's offshore operations and to difficult areas such as the north-eastern states and the interior of Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand.

ex.q: Kolkata port lies inland on the Hugli river, not on the open sea. Why did India need to develop Haldia?
st: Kolkata is a riverine port; the Hugli brings silt, so the channel must be dredged constantly.
Big ships find it hard to reach Kolkata, and traffic kept growing.
Haldia, closer to the sea, was developed as a subsidiary port to relieve the pressure on Kolkata.
ex.a: To relieve the growing pressure on Kolkata, a silt-prone inland riverine port, Haldia was developed as a subsidiary port.

topics.rl: When a helicopter drops supplies to a remote village in Arunachal Pradesh, it is often Pawan Hans — airways reach where roads cannot.

topics.h: A postcard, a radio programme and a phone call all carry messages — and buying and selling with other countries keeps the economy humming!
p: The Indian postal network is the largest in the world. First-class mail (cards and envelopes) is airlifted between stations, covering both land and air. Second-class mail (book packets, registered newspapers and periodicals) is carried by surface mail, covering land and water transport.
To deliver mail quickly in large towns and cities, six mail channels were introduced: Rajdhani Channel, Metro Channel, Green Channel, Business Channel, Bulk Mail Channel and Periodical Channel.

Mass communication includes radio, television, newspapers and films. All India Radio broadcasts in national, regional and local languages; Doordarshan is the national television channel. The Central Board of Film Certification certifies both Indian and foreign films.

Trade is the exchange of goods among people, states and countries. Local trade is carried on within cities, towns and villages; trade between two or more states is state-level trade; trade between countries is international trade. The advancement of international trade is an index of a country's economic prosperity — its economic barometer.

Balance of trade is the difference between a country's exports and imports. When exports are more than imports, it is a favourable balance of trade; when imports are more than exports, it is unfavourable. Tourism earns foreign exchange, supports local handicrafts and promotes national integration and international understanding of our culture and heritage.

ex.q: Country A exports goods worth ₹500 crore and imports goods worth ₹650 crore in a year. Is its balance of trade favourable or unfavourable?
st: Balance of trade = exports − imports.
₹500 crore − ₹650 crore = −₹150 crore.
Imports are more than exports, so the balance is unfavourable.
ex.a: Unfavourable, because imports (₹650 crore) are more than exports (₹500 crore) by ₹150 crore.

topics.rl: When foreign tourists buy a Channapatna wooden toy or a Madhubani painting, tourism supports local artisans and brings foreign exchange to India.

qa.q: Which of these is a biotic resource?
qa.e: Biotic resources come from the biosphere and have life. Livestock are living animals; the others are non-living.

qa.q: Why are coal and petroleum called non-renewable resources?
qa.a: They take millions of years to form
qa.e: Fossil fuels form over very long geological periods, so once used up they cannot be replaced in a human lifetime.

qa.q: A pond in a village is used by all the families living there. On the basis of ownership, it is a/an:
qa.e: Resources that are open to all members of a community, like village ponds and grazing grounds, are community-owned.

qa.q: Rajasthan and Gujarat have huge possibilities for wind and solar energy that are not yet fully used. These are examples of:
qa.e: Resources found in a region but not yet fully utilised are potential resources.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a condition for something to become a resource?
qa.a: It must be rare in nature
qa.e: The three conditions are technological accessibility, economic feasibility and cultural acceptability. Rarity is not a condition — air and sunlight are plentiful yet are resources.

qa.q: Classifying resources as renewable and non-renewable is done on the basis of:
qa.e: Exhaustibility asks whether a resource can be renewed or will get used up.

qa.q: Water contains hydrogen, which could be a great fuel, but we lack the technology to use it widely for this purpose. Hydrogen in water is therefore an example of:
qa.e: Stock is material that can satisfy human needs but cannot yet be used because we lack the right technology.

qa.q: Water stored in a dam that can be used with existing technology for future needs belongs to which category?
qa.e: Reserves are a part of the stock that can be used with present technology but are kept for future use, like water in dams and forests.

qa.q: In which year was the Earth Summit held at Rio de Janeiro?
qa.e: The Earth Summit met at Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in June 1992 and adopted Agenda 21.

qa.q: Which report, published in 1987, introduced the concept of 'sustainable development'?
qa.e: The Brundtland Commission Report of 1987 introduced sustainable development; Agenda 21 came later, in 1992.

qa.q: What is the main aim of Agenda 21?
qa.e: Agenda 21 aims at global sustainable development by fighting environmental damage, poverty and disease through cooperation.

qa.q: 'Every local government should draw its own local Agenda 21.' What does this mean?
qa.a: Towns and villages should make their own plans for sustainable development
qa.e: Agenda 21 wants sustainable development planned at every level, including local bodies.

qa.q: What is the FIRST step in resource planning in India?
qa.e: We must first know what resources exist and how much — by surveying, mapping and estimating — before we can plan their use.

qa.q: Development means using resources without harming the environment and without compromising the needs of future generations. This is called:
qa.e: This is the definition of sustainable development.

qa.q: 'There is enough for everybody's need and not for anybody's greed.' Who said this?
qa.e: Mahatma Gandhi said this to show that over-use for greed, not genuine need, causes resource depletion.

qa.q: When resources pile up in the hands of a few people, what problem does it create?
qa.a: Society gets divided into haves and have-nots
qa.e: Accumulation of resources in a few hands divides society into the rich (haves) and the poor (have-nots).

qa.q: About what percentage of India's land area is plains?
qa.e: About 43% of India's land is plains, 30% mountains and 27% plateaus.

qa.q: Land that has been left uncultivated for more than 5 agricultural years is called:
qa.e: More than 5 years without cultivation makes it culturable waste land; 1–5 years is 'other than current fallow'.

qa.q: What is 'current fallow' land?
qa.a: Land left uncultivated for one agricultural year or less
qa.e: Current fallow is land rested for one agricultural year or less to regain fertility.

qa.q: Gross cropped area is equal to:
qa.a: Net sown area + area sown more than once in an agricultural year
qa.e: Gross cropped area counts a field once for every crop sown on it in the year, so it adds the area sown more than once to the net sown area.

qa.q: How has over-irrigation degraded land in Punjab and Haryana?
qa.a: By causing waterlogging, which increases salinity and alkalinity of the soil
qa.e: Too much irrigation causes waterlogging; salts rise to the surface, making the soil saline and alkaline.

qa.q: According to the National Forest Policy (1952), what share of India's geographical area should ideally be under forests?
qa.e: The 1952 policy set a desired forest cover of 33% of the geographical area; India's actual forest area is well below this.

qa.q: In which state is the net sown area more than 80% of the total area?
qa.e: Punjab and Haryana have over 80% of their area as net sown area; Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram and Manipur have less than 10%.

qa.q: Which measure helps to check land degradation in arid areas?
qa.a: Stabilising sand dunes by growing thorny bushes
qa.e: Thorny bushes and shelter belts hold the sand in place; the other options actually cause degradation.

qa.q: Black soil is also known as:
qa.e: Black soil is called regur or black cotton soil. Khadar and bangar are types of alluvial soil.

qa.q: Black soil in the Deccan was formed from:
qa.e: The parent material of black soil is the volcanic lava of the Deccan trap region.

qa.q: Why does red soil look red?
qa.a: Because of iron diffused in crystalline and metamorphic rocks
qa.e: Iron diffused through the crystalline and metamorphic parent rock gives red soil its colour; it looks yellow when hydrated.

qa.q: How is khadar different from bangar?
qa.a: Khadar is newer alluvium and more fertile
qa.e: Khadar is newer alluvium with finer particles and higher fertility; bangar is older and has more kankar nodules.

qa.q: Laterite soil develops in areas with:
qa.a: High temperature and heavy rainfall causing intense leaching
qa.e: Heavy rain in hot regions washes nutrients down (leaching), forming laterite soil.

qa.q: The ravines of the Chambal basin are an example of:
qa.e: Running water cuts deep gullies in clayey soil, making the land unfit for farming — called bad land; in the Chambal basin these are ravines.

qa.q: In which region is terrace farming well developed in India?
qa.e: Terraces are cut on steep hill slopes, and they are well developed in the western and central Himalayas.

qa.q: What is the purpose of strip cropping?
qa.a: Strips of grass between crops break the force of the wind
qa.e: In strip cropping, grass strips are left between crop strips to reduce wind erosion.

qa.q: What does 'biodiversity' mean?
qa.a: The variety of living organisms in an area
qa.e: Biodiversity is the variety of life — plants, animals and micro-organisms — and their ecosystems.

qa.q: Why are forests called 'primary producers'?
qa.a: Other living beings depend on them for food
qa.e: Green plants make food by photosynthesis, and all other living beings depend on them directly or indirectly.

qa.q: In which year was the Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act implemented?
qa.e: The Act was implemented in 1972; Project Tiger followed in 1973.

qa.q: Which of these was a provision of the Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act?
qa.a: Banning hunting and restricting trade in wildlife
qa.e: The Act banned hunting, gave legal protection to habitats and restricted trade in wildlife.

qa.q: Why is conserving genetic diversity important for farming?
qa.a: It helps breed better crop varieties
qa.e: A wide variety of genes gives scientists and farmers choices to breed crops that resist pests, drought and disease.

qa.q: Which animal is also called the Kashmir stag?
qa.e: The hangul is the Kashmir stag, a deer found in Jammu and Kashmir.

qa.q: Which of these is a life-support system that conservation helps to preserve?
qa.e: Conservation preserves the natural systems — water, air and soil — that all life depends on.

qa.q: A gharial is a:
qa.e: The gharial is a fish-eating crocodile with a long, narrow snout, found in rivers like the Chambal; it has been given special protection.

qa.q: In which year was Project Tiger launched?
qa.e: Project Tiger began in 1973, a year after the Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a major threat to tigers mentioned in your textbook?
qa.e: Poaching, shrinking habitats and loss of prey threaten tigers; planting trees improves their habitat.

qa.q: Sundarbans National Park is located in:
qa.e: The Sundarbans, the mangrove delta of the Ganga and Brahmaputra, is in West Bengal.

qa.q: Periyar Tiger Reserve is in which state?
qa.e: Periyar Tiger Reserve is in Kerala, in the Western Ghats.

qa.q: Which type of forest makes up more than half of India's total forest land?
qa.e: More than half of India's forest land is reserved forest; about one-third is protected forest.

qa.q: About what share of India's forest area is protected forest?
qa.e: Protected forests are almost one-third of the total forest area.

qa.q: Forests and wastelands that belong to the government, private individuals and communities, other than reserved and protected forests, are called:
qa.e: Unclassed forests are other forests and wastelands owned by government, private individuals and communities.

qa.q: Which state has the largest area under permanent forests?
qa.e: Madhya Pradesh has the largest area under permanent forests (reserved + protected).

qa.q: Which movement in the Himalayas successfully resisted deforestation?
qa.e: The Chipko movement resisted the cutting of trees in the Himalayas and promoted community afforestation.

qa.q: Joint Forest Management (JFM) began in 1988 in which state?
qa.e: Odisha passed the first resolution for Joint Forest Management in 1988.

qa.q: Under JFM, what do village communities receive in return for protecting forests?
qa.a: Non-timber forest produce and a share of timber
qa.e: Villagers get non-timber forest produce and a share of the timber harvested through successful protection.

qa.q: The Bhairodev Dakav 'Sonchuri' was declared by villagers of which district?
qa.e: Five villages in Alwar district of Rajasthan declared about 1,200 hectares as the Bhairodev Dakav 'Sonchuri'.

qa.q: Which communities of Chota Nagpur worship the mahua and kadamba trees?
qa.e: The Mundas and Santhals of the Chota Nagpur region worship mahua and kadamba trees and protect them.

qa.q: What did the Beej Bachao Andolan in Tehri and Navdanya show?
qa.a: Diverse crops can be grown without synthetic chemicals
qa.e: They showed that diversified crop production without synthetic chemicals is economically viable.

qa.q: In Bishnoi villages of Rajasthan, which animals roam freely and are protected by the community?
qa.e: Herds of blackbuck, nilgai and peacocks live as part of Bishnoi village life, and no one harms them.

qa.q: What are sacred groves?
qa.a: Forest patches protected because of local beliefs
qa.e: Sacred groves are patches of forest left untouched because people believe them to be sacred; interfering with them is banned by tradition.

qa.q: Fresh water is continually renewed by:
qa.e: The hydrological (water) cycle of evaporation, condensation and precipitation keeps renewing fresh water.

qa.q: Which is the most common reason for water scarcity in India, according to your textbook?
qa.a: Over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access to water
qa.e: Scarcity is mostly caused by over-use and unequal access, not only by low rainfall.

qa.q: How does growing food production for a large population add to water scarcity?
qa.a: More land is irrigated, including in the dry season
qa.e: Feeding more people needs more irrigated land and dry-season crops, which use large amounts of water.

qa.q: Pumping out too much groundwater through tube wells leads to:
qa.e: Pumping faster than rain can recharge the ground lowers the water table.

qa.q: A river flows through a town, but its water is full of factory waste and sewage. This is an example of scarcity caused by:
qa.e: Even when water is available, pollution makes it unfit to use, causing scarcity.

qa.q: Sringaverapura, near Prayagraj, had a water harvesting system in the 1st century BCE that channelled the floodwater of which river?
qa.e: Sringaverapura near Prayagraj channelled the floodwater of the Ganga.

qa.q: Bhopal Lake, one of the largest artificial lakes of its time, was built in which century?
qa.e: Bhopal Lake was built in the 11th century.

qa.q: How do industries add to the demand for water?
qa.a: They use water in production and need power, much of which comes from hydroelectricity
qa.e: Industries are heavy users of water and also need energy, a large part of which comes from hydroelectric power.

qa.q: Who called dams the 'temples of modern India'?
qa.e: Jawaharlal Nehru called dams the 'temples of modern India' because they would help both farming and industry grow.

qa.q: The Bhakra Nangal project is in which river basin?
qa.e: Bhakra Nangal is in the Sutlej-Beas basin and is used for hydel power and irrigation.

qa.q: The Hirakud project is on which river?
qa.e: Hirakud is on the Mahanadi in Odisha; it combines water conservation with flood control.

qa.q: Why are they called 'multipurpose' river projects?
qa.a: One project serves many uses such as irrigation, power, flood control and water supply
qa.e: A single project serves several purposes at the same time.

qa.q: The Narmada Bachao Andolan raised concerns about which dam?
qa.e: The Narmada Bachao Andolan focused on the Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada, especially the rehabilitation of displaced people and the environment.

qa.q: How does a big dam affect fish in a river?
qa.a: It blocks fish migration and changes their habitat
qa.e: Dams break the river's natural flow, so fish cannot migrate freely and their habitat changes.

qa.q: Why does a reservoir slowly lose its storage capacity?
qa.a: Sediment settles at the bottom of the reservoir
qa.e: Rivers carry sediment, which settles in the still water of the reservoir and fills it up over time.

qa.q: Over-irrigation from canals of big dams can lead to:
qa.e: Too much irrigation raises the water table and brings salts to the surface, making soil saline.

qa.q: 'Guls' or 'kuls' are diversion channels found in:
qa.e: In the hilly western Himalayas, people built guls or kuls to divert stream water for farming.

qa.q: What were 'tankas' in Rajasthan?
qa.a: Underground tanks for storing rooftop rainwater
qa.e: Tankas were underground tanks, often inside the house or courtyard, linked to the sloping roof by a pipe.

qa.q: In Rajasthan, the rainwater stored in tankas was called 'palar pani'. Why was it valued so much?
qa.a: It was considered the purest form of natural water
qa.e: Palar pani was considered the purest natural water and was relied on until the next rains.

qa.q: Which was the first Indian state to make rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for all houses?
qa.e: Tamil Nadu made rooftop rainwater harvesting structures compulsory for all houses, with penalties for defaulters.

qa.q: Bamboo drip irrigation, about 200 years old, is practised in:
qa.e: In Meghalaya, bamboo pipes carry water from streams and springs downhill to plants, using gravity.

qa.q: Inundation channels were developed in the floodplains of Bengal to:
qa.e: People built inundation channels to carry floodwater to irrigate fields.

qa.q: Khadins in Jaisalmer and johads in Rajasthan were used to:
qa.a: Store rainwater in fields and moisten the soil for crops
qa.e: Agricultural fields were turned into rain-fed storage areas so that water stood and moistened the soil.

qa.q: Which of these is an advantage of rooftop rainwater harvesting in cities?
qa.a: It recharges groundwater and reduces dependence on tankers
qa.e: Rooftop harvesting stores rain or sends it into the ground, raising groundwater and reducing shortages.

qa.q: Which tools are typical of primitive subsistence farming?
qa.e: Primitive subsistence farming uses simple tools like the hoe, dao and digging sticks with family labour.

qa.q: Slash and burn agriculture is called 'jhumming' in:
qa.e: Jhumming is the name used in the north-eastern states; it is bewar or dahiya in Madhya Pradesh and podu or penda in Andhra Pradesh.

qa.q: In slash and burn farming, why does the farmer shift to a new patch of land?
qa.a: The soil of the old patch loses its fertility
qa.e: Without fertilisers, soil fertility falls after a few years, so farmers clear a fresh patch and let nature restore the old one.

qa.q: Intensive subsistence farming is practised in areas with:
qa.e: With many people and little land, farmers use labour and inputs intensively to get the most from small plots.

qa.q: Which inputs are the main feature of commercial farming?
qa.a: HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, insecticides and pesticides
qa.e: Commercial farming uses modern inputs to obtain higher productivity for the market.

qa.q: Rice is a commercial crop in Punjab and Haryana, but in Odisha it is mainly a:
qa.e: In Odisha most rice is grown for the farmer's own family; in Punjab and Haryana it is grown largely for sale.

qa.q: Which of these is a feature of plantation farming?
qa.a: A single crop is grown on a large area
qa.e: Plantations grow one crop on a large estate using capital and migrant labour, linked to industries.

qa.q: Tea plantations in India are mainly found in:
qa.e: Tea is a major plantation crop of Assam and North Bengal (Darjeeling and Jalpaiguri).

qa.q: Rabi crops are harvested during:
qa.e: Rabi crops are sown in October–December and harvested in April–June.

qa.q: Which of these is a rabi crop?
qa.e: Gram is sown in winter and harvested in summer, so it is a rabi crop. Paddy, jute and bajra are kharif crops.

qa.q: Kharif crops are sown:
qa.a: With the onset of the monsoon
qa.e: Kharif crops are sown when the monsoon arrives and harvested in September–October.

qa.q: Which of these is a kharif crop?
qa.e: Cotton is sown at the start of the monsoon and is a kharif crop; wheat, mustard and peas are rabi crops.

qa.q: The zaid season comes:
qa.a: In summer, between the rabi and kharif seasons
qa.e: Zaid is a short summer season between the rabi harvest and the kharif sowing.

qa.q: Which crops are typical of the zaid season?
qa.e: Watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables and fodder crops are grown in the zaid season.

qa.q: Aus, aman and boro are three crops of paddy grown in a year in:
qa.e: Assam, West Bengal and Odisha grow three paddy crops a year — aus, aman and boro.

qa.q: What helps rabi crops grow well in north India during winter?
qa.e: Winter rainfall from western temperate cyclones helps rabi crops in the north.

qa.q: What annual rainfall does rice need (without irrigation)?
qa.e: Rice grows well with high temperature, high humidity and annual rainfall above 100 cm; in drier areas irrigation is used.

qa.q: How is rice grown in Punjab and Haryana, which get less rainfall?
qa.a: With canal irrigation and tube wells
qa.e: Canal irrigation and tube wells have made rice cultivation possible in low-rainfall areas like Punjab and Haryana.

qa.q: Wheat requires a cool growing season and bright sunshine at the time of:
qa.e: Bright sunshine is needed when the wheat grain ripens.

qa.q: Which are the two important wheat-growing zones of India?
qa.a: Ganga-Satluj plains and the black soil region of the Deccan
qa.e: Wheat grows mainly in the Ganga-Satluj plains in the north-west and the black soil region of the Deccan.

qa.q: Which millet is the third most important food crop with respect to area and production?
qa.e: Jowar is the third most important food crop by area and production.

qa.q: Ragi is valued because it is very rich in:
qa.e: Ragi is very rich in iron, calcium, other micro-nutrients and roughage.

qa.q: Maize grows well in temperatures between:
qa.e: Maize needs temperatures between 21°C and 27°C and grows well in old alluvial soil.

qa.q: Why are pulses grown in rotation with other crops?
qa.a: Being leguminous, they fix nitrogen from the air and restore soil fertility
qa.e: Leguminous pulses fix atmospheric nitrogen, improving the soil for the next crop.

qa.q: Sugarcane needs a temperature of:
qa.e: Sugarcane needs a hot and humid climate with temperatures of 21°C to 27°C and 75–100 cm of rainfall.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT obtained from sugarcane?
qa.e: Sugarcane gives sugar, gur, khandsari and molasses; linseed oil comes from the linseed oilseed.

qa.q: Which oilseed is grown as a kharif crop?
qa.e: Groundnut is a kharif crop; mustard and linseed are rabi crops; gram is a pulse, not an oilseed.

qa.q: Coffee cultivation in India was first introduced on the:
qa.e: The Arabica variety, first brought from Yemen, was first grown on the Baba Budan Hills.

qa.q: Which climate suits tea cultivation?
qa.a: Warm, moist and frost-free climate with frequent showers
qa.e: Tea needs a warm, moist, frost-free climate with frequent, evenly spread showers so that tender leaves keep growing.

qa.q: Rubber needs rainfall of more than:
qa.e: Rubber needs a moist, humid climate with rainfall above 200 cm and temperature above 25°C.

qa.q: How many frost-free days does cotton need?
qa.e: Cotton needs high temperature, light rainfall or irrigation, 210 frost-free days and bright sunshine.

qa.q: Which crop is known as the 'golden fibre'?
qa.e: Jute is called the golden fibre because of its golden colour and value.

qa.q: Which of these is a ferrous mineral?
qa.e: Ferrous minerals are those used in making iron and steel, like iron ore and manganese. Copper and bauxite are non-ferrous; mica is non-metallic.

qa.q: Which of these is a non-metallic mineral?
qa.e: Mica, salt, potash, sulphur and limestone are non-metallic minerals.

qa.q: Coal, petroleum and natural gas are classified as:
qa.e: Coal, petroleum and natural gas are energy minerals because they are used as fuels.

qa.q: Gold, silver and platinum belong to which group of metallic minerals?
qa.e: They are precious metallic minerals because they are rare and valuable.

qa.q: What is an 'ore'?
qa.a: A mineral mixed with other elements, concentrated enough to be mined profitably
qa.e: An ore is an accumulation of a mineral mixed with other elements; it is worth mining only if the concentration is high enough.

qa.q: Bauxite is formed by:
qa.a: Decomposition of surface rocks and removal of soluble materials
qa.e: Bauxite forms when surface rocks decompose and the soluble parts are washed away, leaving a residue with aluminium.

qa.q: Placer deposits found in the sands of valley floors may contain:
qa.e: Placer deposits are alluvial deposits in river sands that may contain gold, silver, tin and platinum.

qa.q: Rat-hole mining, declared illegal by the National Green Tribunal, is practised in:
qa.e: Rat-hole mining in long narrow tunnels has been done in Jowai and Cherapunjee in Meghalaya.

qa.q: Which iron ore is the finest, with up to 70% iron?
qa.e: Magnetite has up to 70% iron and excellent magnetic qualities; hematite has 50–60%.

qa.q: About how much manganese is needed to make one tonne of steel?
qa.e: Nearly 10 kg of manganese is required to manufacture one tonne of steel.

qa.q: Iron ore from the Bailadila hills is exported through which port?
qa.e: Bailadila's high-grade hematite is exported through Visakhapatnam port.

qa.q: Kudremukh, a 100% export unit for iron ore, is in which state?
qa.e: Kudremukh in the Western Ghats of Karnataka sends ore as slurry through a pipeline to a port near Mangaluru.

qa.q: Bauxite is the ore of which metal?
qa.e: Aluminium is obtained from bauxite.

qa.q: Which mineral is used mainly as an insulator in electrical and electronic industries?
qa.e: Mica has excellent di-electric strength and resists high voltage, so it is used as an insulator.

qa.q: Balaghat, Khetri and Singhbhum are known for which mineral?
qa.e: Balaghat (MP), Khetri (Rajasthan) and Singhbhum (Jharkhand) are major copper-producing areas.

qa.q: Which is a health hazard faced by miners?
qa.a: Lung diseases from inhaling dust and fumes
qa.e: Miners breathe dust and harmful fumes, which can cause pulmonary (lung) diseases.

qa.q: Which is the highest quality hard coal?
qa.e: Anthracite is the highest quality hard coal; peat and lignite are low-grade.

qa.q: Lignite, a low-grade brown coal, is mainly found at:
qa.e: The principal lignite reserves are at Neyveli in Tamil Nadu, used for generating electricity.

qa.q: About how old is Gondwana coal, according to your textbook?
qa.e: Gondwana coal is about 200 million years old; tertiary coal is about 55 million years old.

qa.q: Tertiary coal is found mainly in:
qa.e: Tertiary coal occurs in Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland.

qa.q: Which is the oldest oil-producing state of India?
qa.e: Assam is the oldest oil-producing state, with fields at Digboi, Naharkatiya and Moran-Hugrijan.

qa.q: Why are oil refineries called a 'nodal industry'?
qa.a: They supply raw materials to synthetic textile, fertiliser and chemical industries
qa.e: Refineries act as a node or centre that supplies raw materials to many other industries.

qa.q: The HVJ gas pipeline connects which places?
qa.e: HVJ stands for Hazira–Vijaipur–Jagdishpur; this pipeline carries natural gas to western and northern India.

qa.q: Thermal electricity is generated by using:
qa.e: Thermal power plants burn fossil fuels; hydel power uses running water.

qa.q: Which of these is a non-conventional source of energy?
qa.e: Wind is a non-conventional, renewable source; coal, petroleum and firewood are conventional.

qa.q: The monazite sands of Kerala are rich in:
qa.e: Monazite sands of Kerala are rich in thorium, used for nuclear energy.

qa.q: Where are India's experimental geothermal energy projects located?
qa.a: Parvati valley (Himachal Pradesh) and Puga valley (Ladakh)
qa.e: The two experimental geothermal projects are at Parvati valley near Manikarn and Puga valley in Ladakh.

qa.q: Which areas of India have ideal conditions for tidal energy?
qa.a: Gulf of Khambhat, Gulf of Kachchh and the Sundarbans
qa.e: Tidal energy needs narrow gulfs or deltas with strong tides, such as the Gulf of Khambhat, Gulf of Kachchh and the Sundarbans.

qa.q: What are the twin benefits of a gobar gas plant?
qa.a: Energy and improved quality of manure
qa.e: A gobar gas plant gives biogas for energy and leaves slurry that makes better manure.

qa.q: How does photovoltaic technology work?
qa.a: It converts sunlight directly into electricity
qa.e: Photovoltaic cells convert sunlight directly into electricity.

qa.q: Nuclear energy is obtained by:
